segments.narration: Divers pulled a 2,000-year-old computer from a Roman-era shipwreck. In 1901, sponge divers off Antikythera spotted a strange calcified lump.
segments.visual_query: mediterranean underwater shipwreck scuba diver seabed

segments.narration: Decades later, X-rays revealed over thirty interlocking bronze gears inside. Its precision rivaled 18th-century clockwork.
segments.visual_query: ancient greek corroded bronze artifact museum

segments.narration: How could ancient builders craft technology this advanced fifteen centuries early? No other device like it existed on Earth.
segments.visual_query: ancient greece temple ruins aegean coastline

segments.narration: 3D scans finally decoded hidden Greek inscriptions inside the bronze. It was a hand-cranked mechanical calculator built to track planetary motion and predict eclipses.
Greek engineers built a functional mechanical computer over a thousand years before modern history thought possible.

accuracy_flags.claim: The Antikythera mechanism was recovered from an ancient Greek shipwreck by sponge divers off the coast of Antikythera in 1901.
accuracy_flags.note: The reference articles state that the ship was a Roman cargo ship and a Roman-era shipwreck, rather than a Greek shipwreck.

verdicts.claim: The Antikythera mechanism was recovered from an ancient Greek shipwreck by sponge divers off the coast of Antikythera in 1901.
verdicts.note: The reference articles state that the ship was a Roman cargo ship and a Roman-era shipwreck, rather than a Greek shipwreck.
verdicts.correction: Divers pulled a 2,000-year-old computer from a Roman-era shipwreck. In 1901, sponge divers off Antikythera spotted a strange calcified lump.

verdicts.claim: X-ray imaging revealed at least 30 interlocking bronze gears inside the Antikythera mechanism.
verdicts.note: Reference text confirms X-ray imaging was used and revealed 37 meshing bronze gears inside the mechanism.

verdicts.claim: No other mechanical artifact with comparable gear complexity is known from the ancient world for over a thousand years following its construction.
verdicts.note: Reference text confirms that machines of similar complexity did not appear again for around 1,500 years (fifteen centuries).

verdicts.claim: High-resolution computed tomography decoded hidden inscriptions on the Antikythera mechanism revealing it calculated planetary motions and solar eclipses.
verdicts.note: Reference text states high-resolution scanning and computer X-ray tomography decoded faint inscriptions on the device, showing it tracked planetary motions and predicted eclipses.

verdicts.claim: The Antikythera mechanism was built between 200 BCE and 60 BCE, predating similar mechanical gear technology by more than a millennium.
verdicts.note: Reference text dates construction between 205 BC and 60 BC and notes that similar complex technology did not re-emerge for around 1,500 years.
